summary: This is a position paper giving the author's personal views on how quality of service should fit into Information-Centric Networking protocols such as CCNx or NDN. It argues these need an approach different from TCP/IP, proposes design patterns for classification and differentiated treatment, and considers caches as resources. It is not an ICNRG product.

plainLanguage.summary: Information-Centric Networking (ICN) protocols ask for data by name and let every router remember what it has seen, so they work differently from the address-based TCP/IP model. RFC 9064 argues that quality of service, which decides which traffic gets better treatment, should be designed for those differences instead of copied from IP. It proposes principles and example treatments, not a finished protocol.

subtitle: How quality of service should work in information-centric networks, and why IP's approach does not fit.

tldr.problem: Information-Centric Networking protocols such as CCNx and NDN differ from TCP/IP in ways that make IP's quality-of-service machinery a poor fit, and they have had little deployment so far to force a choice.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9064 argues for a QoS approach built on ICN properties: name hierarchies for classification, consumer control of link and forwarding resources, producer and consumer influence on cache allocation, and network operator control over cache resources against service level agreements.
tldr.outcome: The document is a position paper that sketches design patterns and example treatments, leaving the concrete protocol machinery to later specifications. It is published as an individual IRTF submission with the support of the ICN research group.

today: RFC 9064 is an Informational position paper published in June 2021 by an individual IRTF member rather than by the ICN research group. It has not been obsoleted or updated. The concrete protocol machinery it leaves open is expected in supplementary specifications.

sections.title: Why ICN Needs Its Own Quality of Service
sections.content:
This is a position paper recording the author's personal views on how quality of service (QoS) should be accommodated in Information-Centric Networking (ICN) protocols such as Content-Centric Networking (CCNx) or Named Data Networking (NDN). It is not a product of the IRTF Information-Centric Networking Research Group, though it went through a formal Last Call and has the support of the participants in the group.

The starting point is a difference in experience. TCP/IP has over 30 years of accumulated research and engineering into QoS machinery, used with varying success in different environments. ICN protocols have about ten years of research and very little deployment. That gap is the opportunity the author takes: either recapitulate the approaches taken with TCP/IP, such as Intserv and Diffserv, or design something new that fits ICN properties. The paper advocates the second.

The differences that matter for QoS are set out in Table 1 of the document. IP forwards packets without per-packet state, groups flows by address prefix and port, and uses end-to-end congestion control. CCNx and NDN forward with per-packet state, group flows by name prefix, and can use hop-by-hop congestion control. IP has a pure datagram model and asymmetric routing; ICN has a request-response model and symmetric routing, where flow balance guarantees that one Interest provokes a response of no more than one Data packet.

Two limits shape the argument. First, QoS here means managed unfairness: giving better service to some traffic at the expense of others. A QoS mechanism cannot create capacity, and every known scheme has overhead that slightly reduces the resources available for user traffic. Second, QoS only helps in a narrow band of conditions. When resources are lightly loaded it is not needed, because there is neither congestion loss nor much queuing delay. When resources are heavily oversubscribed it does not save the situation. The interesting cases are in between, where a failure can move the network quickly from the first state to the second. The paper also excludes Quality of Experience, which can only be assessed and controlled at the application layer or above.
sections.plainLanguage: Most networks treat all traffic alike, or as nearly alike as they can. Quality of service means deliberately treating some traffic better than others. This RFC argues that Information-Centric Networking, which asks for data by name and lets routers remember what they have seen, should get its own design for that rather than a copy of the IP one.

sections.title: How Interest and Data Messages Move
sections.content:
In NDN and CCNx every protocol interaction is a two-way handshake. A consumer requests named content with an Interest message, which is routed hop by hop through a series of forwarders until it reaches a node holding the requested data. That node is either the producer of the data or a forwarder with a cached copy. The content matching the name in the Interest is returned to the requester over the inverse of the path the Interest travelled.

Forwarding is per-packet stateful. Routing information for choosing the next hop or hops of an Interest comes from a Forwarding Information Base that holds name prefixes rather than IP address prefixes. The conventional lookup is a Longest Name Prefix Match, although controlled flooding and adaptive learning from prior history are also possible.

Each Interest leaves breadcrumbs as state in every forwarder it passes. This state lives in the Pending Interest Table (PIT) and is used to send the returning Data message back to the consumer. Because it is per-packet state, the PIT consumes a large share of memory, especially in forwarders carrying heavy traffic over long round-trip-time paths, which makes it a resource that a QoS scheme can control. A forwarder may also act as a cache, optionally storing a copy of Data messages it has seen in a local Content Store (CS). Data in the CS can answer a matching Interest instead of forwarding it further to the producer.

Congestion control works differently too. The IP family relies exclusively on end-to-end congestion control. CCNx and NDN can use hop-by-hop control, because there is per-Interest and per-Data state at every hop and the outstanding Interests say what the reverse direction will have to carry. Many schemes do this by Interest counting: accepting one Interest implicitly guarantees that there is bandwidth on the reverse link for one Data packet. Other schemes neither count nor police Interests but monitor queues with active queue management and mark returning Data packets that met congestion, which puts the burden on consumers to reduce their Interest rate.

Two properties of ICN make the allocation more accurate and quicker than in IP. The Interest Lifetime bounds the round-trip-time uncertainty for any Interest and Data exchange, so short lifetimes keep the uncertainty small. And a congestion marking scheme like Explicit Congestion Notification can mark returning Data packets when the inverse link gets congested; the downstream forwarder can use that feedback at once and lower the Interest shaping rate after a single link round-trip time, which may allow rate adjustment that is less pessimistic than the Additive Increase, Multiplicative Decrease scheme used on TCP/IP networks.
sections.plainLanguage: A request for named data travels through the network one router at a time. Every router that sees it writes down which way it came, so it can send the answer back the same way. The answer may come from the original publisher or from a router that kept a copy. Because each router knows what is outstanding on its links, it can control congestion link by link instead of waiting for an end-to-end signal.

sections.title: What a QoS Scheme Has to Decide
sections.content:
QoS is achieved through managed unfairness in the allocation of resources inside network elements, particularly the routers that forward ICN packets. The document lists four resources that matter in CCNx and NDN: communication link capacity, used for buffering queued packets; CS capacity, used to hold cached data; forwarder memory, used for the PIT; and compute capacity, used for forwarding packets, including the cost of FIB lookups. IP has fewer resource types to manage: it has no cache in its routers, forwarder memory is only needed in output-buffered designs, and its compute cost for forwarding is arguably much cheaper than in ICN.

For those resources, any QoS scheme has to settle two questions. First, how to create equivalence classes, also called flows, of traffic to which different treatments apply. Second, what the possible treatments are and how those treatments map onto the resource allocation algorithms.

Two practical limits shape the answers. The number of equivalence classes a network element can track at the same time is bounded by its memory and by the processing capacity needed for the lookups. Very fine-grained classes are possible in principle but not globally, because of the scaling limits of core routers, so it is wise either to restrict the range of classes or to allow them to be aggregated, trading accuracy in policing traffic against the ability to scale. The other limit is that the expressiveness of treatments is constrained by protocol encoding and by algorithm design. IP has only six Type of Service bits available for Diffserv treatments, but the more important question is whether practical traffic policing, queuing and pacing algorithms exist that can be combined to support a rich set of treatments.
sections.plainLanguage: Quality of service has to answer two things: which traffic goes in which group, and what each group gets. The groups have to be few enough to track at full speed in a busy router, and the treatments have to be things the router can actually enforce with its queues and its processing power.

sections.title: What ICN Changes
sections.content:
The paper sets out several reasons why ICN can support richer QoS than IP. Hierarchical names are a much richer basis for equivalence classes than the IP 5-tuple. An IP address can only separate traffic by topology down to the granularity of hosts, and cannot express computational instances or sets of data; ports give some per-instance separation but tend to be coarse and ephemeral. Tokenized, variable-length hierarchical names let traffic classes follow the structure of an application namespace, as coarsely or finely as the application wants.

Because names are not tied to topology, QoS is not pre-bound to the network topology. Multicast and multipath environments can be handled directly, instead of needing multicast with coarse class-based scheduling or the complex signalling that RSVP-TE needs for point-to-multipoint MPLS. ICN also needs less state: even in the worst case it needs state on the order of the number of active Interest and Data exchanges, because state can be created when an Interest arrives and removed once the data has been returned, whereas Intserv needs flow signalling on the order of the number of flows.

The wire format is not a limit either. NDN and CCNx are entirely Type-Length-Value based, so one or more new fields can carry QoS treatment information without the six-bit ceiling of the IP TOS field. That opens treatments IP has no way to express, such as trying hard to deliver reliably even at the expense of delay or bandwidth. Such a treatment could invoke native ICN mechanisms: retransmitting inside the network in response to hop-by-hop errors reported by upstream forwarders; trying multiple paths to multiple content sources, in parallel or in series; giving higher precedence to short-term caching to recover from downstream errors; and coordinating cache use with forwarding resources.

IP has three forwarding semantics, with different QoS needs: unicast, anycast and multicast. ICN has a single forwarding semantic, so the same machinery can be applied to any request and response, whether the forwarder picks one next hop, tries next hops serially, uses them in parallel, or floods. The pull-based model also avoids several multicast QoS problems that IP has.

Caching is the last difference, and it is the one the paper treats most carefully. IP routers have no cache; ICN forwarders do, so cache resources need their own allocation rules and their own treatments, which are unlikely to resemble the ones used for links. CCNx already has two cache directives on Data messages: ExpiryTime, after which a cached Content Object must no longer be used to answer an Interest, and Recommended Cache Time, after which the publisher considers the object of low value to cache. Flow classifiers can partition the Content Store softly or hard between classes. Cached content for one class can be treated as fate shared, so objects are purged as a group rather than one at a time, which recovers cache space faster and at lower overhead than per-object replacement when a cache is under extreme pressure and in danger of thrashing.
sections.plainLanguage: Names give finer and more natural traffic groups than IP addresses and ports, and they do not tie a group to one place in the network, so the same class can be served along many paths. The messages are also flexible enough to carry new treatment fields, and routers that cache content need rules for that cache space as well as for their links.

sections.title: Strawman Principles for an ICN QoS Architecture
sections.content:
The paper closes with principles meant to guide later specification work. They are written as a bulleted list of directives in the source.

  • Define equivalence classes using the name hierarchy rather than creating an independent traffic class definition, so the classes follow the structure of the application namespace and can be decomposed hierarchically.
  • Put consumers in control of link and forwarding resource allocation. Allocations for link buffering and for forwarding memory and CPU should be based on Interest arrivals, which gives early congestion feedback and lets the reverse link be scheduled in advance. It also makes enforcement of a treatment a single-ended problem at the consumer and avoids spending resources on data that will be dropped at a bottleneck.
  • Allow producers to influence the allocation of cache resources, so that Interests can be answered from caches before they reach the producer, shedding load, and so that transient producer or link outages close to the producer can be survived.
  • Allow consumers to influence the allocation of cache resources, to reduce latency, to survive transient outages of a producer or of links near the consumer, and, where a mobile consumer is likely to move within a round-trip time, to have data cached preferentially at a join point or rendezvous point of the topology.
  • Give network operators the ability to match customer service level agreements to cache resource availability, since operators provide the storage and are the ultimate arbiters of how it is managed. They also want caches to reduce congestion hotspots on hosted producers, to act as short-term retransmission buffers that improve Interest satisfaction rates, and to improve latency and reliability for mobile consumers.
  • Rethink how to specify traffic treatments rather than copying Diffserv.

The paper gives three example treatments. A burst treatment lets an initial Interest state an aggregate data size so that link capacity can be allocated for a large burst of exchanges, with the Interest rejected at any hop if the resources are not available. A reliable treatment affects the preference for allocating PIT space for the Interest and CS space for the Data, improving the robustness of delivery in constrained environments. A search treatment tries many paths, in parallel or in series, to many content sources within the Interest Lifetime, at the cost of extra bandwidth; it can encode a trade-off between breadth-first and depth-first search and bounds on total resource expenditure.

Section 7.1 asks whether Intserv-like traffic control could give ICN richer semantics, and identifies three capabilities that Diffserv-like treatments lack whatever their sophistication. The first is the ability to describe traffic flows in a mathematically meaningful way, through parameters such as average rate, peak rate and maximum burst size, held in a traffic specification (TSPEC) that can be placed in whatever protocol needs it. The second is admission control, where the requester learns before introducing traffic whether the network has agreed to provide the requested treatment, with the side effect that the network installs state to police and shape the traffic and isolate it from the behaviour of other traffic. The third is the ability to state the permissible degree of divergence between requested and actual handling, which Intserv provides as the controlled load service, allowing stochastic deviation like an unloaded path, and the guaranteed service, which conforms to the TSPEC deterministically at the cost of very conservative resource allocation. The author takes no position on whether ICN needs these; carrying a TSPEC in a new Interest field would be straightforward, but managing different traffic specifications for Interests of the same class would be substantial, and admission control is likely to be as heavyweight as it is with RSVP, because next-hop selection is not confined to single paths and state would have to be installed at multiple producers over multiple paths.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed principles put the consumer in charge of how much traffic the network carries, and give producers and consumers a say in how cached copies are used. Network operators keep control of the storage they provide. The example treatments show what ICN can ask for that IP cannot, such as spending more bandwidth to find a copy of something, or reserving space to make delivery more dependable.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Interactions
sections.content:
QoS addresses relationships among traffic rather than the inherent characteristics of the traffic itself, so it neither enhances nor degrades the security and privacy properties of the data being carried, as long as the machinery does not alter or compromise the basic security properties of the associated protocols. It can, however, amplify existing threats to network traffic.

An attacker able to manipulate the QoS treatments of traffic can mount a more focused, and potentially more effective, denial-of-service attack by suppressing performance on the traffic being targeted. The architecture here assumes that QoS treatments are manipulable hop by hop, so any on-path adversary can cause damage. The paper notes, however, that in basic ICN an on-path attacker can already drop, delay or misroute traffic independently of any QoS machinery.

There is also a privacy consequence. When equivalence classes of traffic are explicitly revealed through names or other fields in packets, an attacker has one more handle for discovering the linkability of multiple requests.
sections.plainLanguage: Treating some traffic better does not by itself make that traffic safer or less private. But a mechanism that lets anyone on the path change the treatment of a flow can be used to degrade a target flow on purpose, and a name that spells out which class a request belongs to gives an observer a way to link requests together.
